links.outcome: Reader diagnostic accuracy with versus without LLM assistance, and overreliance by expertise
links.effect: Accuracy rose from 56.3% to 65.6% for thoracic radiologists and 42.4% to 58.5% for residents; residents switched to an incorrect diagnosis after misleading LLM output more often (60.6% vs 32.4%).
links.quote: Residents, compared with thoracic radiologists, had a greater rate of accepting LLM-favored diagnoses (73.2% vs 48.9%; p < .001), including a greater rate of switching to an incorrect diagnosis after a misleading LLM output (60.6% vs 32.4%; p = .009).

links.outcome: Rate of users accepting or switching to incorrect diagnoses after misleading LLM output
links.effect: Residents accepted LLM-favored diagnoses more than thoracic radiologists (73.2% vs 48.9%) and switched to incorrect diagnosis after misleading output more (60.6% vs 32.4%).
links.quote: Residents, compared with thoracic radiologists, had a greater rate of accepting LLM-favored diagnoses (73.2% vs 48.9%; p < .001), including a greater rate of switching to an incorrect diagnosis after a misleading LLM output (60.6% vs 32.4%; p = .009).

links.outcome: Human-LLM team accuracy versus reader-alone and LLM-alone accuracy
links.effect: LLM accuracy was 52.7% with images and 63.9% with reader descriptions; reader accuracy improved between sessions, more for residents (16.1 vs 9.2 percentage points; p = .02).
links.quote: Improvement in accuracy between sessions was greater for residents than thoracic radiologists (16.1 vs 9.2 percentage points; p = .02).
